text: In Anthropic's own internal research evaluation, its multi-agent research system substantially outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 baseline.
note: Primary source (Anthropic engineering blog) states 90.2% gain; eval is internal, unpublished, and not compute-matched (multi-agent ~15x chat tokens), so medium confidence that it generalizes; no independent replication found.

text: Most of the performance gain of multi-agent research systems is explained by greater token/compute spend rather than by agent structure per se.
note: Anthropic's own BrowseComp analysis: token usage alone explains 80% of variance; Tran & Kiela show MAS gains confounded by test-time compute. No study found showing structure-only gains dominate. Variance-explained is not causal attribution, hence medium.

text: At matched inference cost or token budget, multi-agent research/reasoning systems do not reliably outperform a single well-prompted agent.
note: Two equal-budget studies (Tran & Kiela multi-hop reasoning; MA-Evolve on ALFWorld/WebShop) find no MAS advantage. Google's 260-config study (compute standardized) finds +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning but -39 to -70% on sequential planning. Resolution: matched-budget MAS advantage is task-dependent (decomposable/parallel tasks only); none of these studies are on difficult technical research specifically.

challenges.query: multi-agent outperforms single agent under matched compute budget controlled study research tasks 2026

text: On deep-research report benchmarks (e.g., DeepResearch Bench), dedicated deep-research agents score higher than LLMs given only search tools.
note: DeepResearch Bench (100 PhD-level tasks): best DRA (Gemini DR 48.88 RACE) > best LLM+search (Claude 3.7 w/Search 40.67), but ranking not uniform (Claude w/Search beats Grok Deeper Search). DeepTRACE: DR configs reduce overconfidence yet still have large fractions of unsupported statements. Not compute-matched; LLM-as-judge scoring.

challenges.query: deep research agents evaluation citation accuracy hallucination worse than LLM with search benchmark 2026

text: On difficult ML research replication/engineering benchmarks (PaperBench, MLE-bench), autonomous agents still fall well short of human experts.
note: PaperBench: best agent 21.0% vs ML PhDs 41.4% (48h); humans overtake after 24h. MLE-bench: bronze+ in 16.9% of competitions. RE-Bench contradicts only at short horizons (agents 4x humans at 2h) but humans 2x at 32h; resolution: agents win short budgets, humans win long-horizon hard tasks.

challenges.query: RE-Bench METR AI agents vs human experts ML research engineering 2 hour 8 hour results

text: Giving the same model an agentic scaffold (iterative tool use / longer horizon) improves results on hard ML research tasks compared to a less agentic scaffold.
note: Same model gains with more agentic scaffolds: PaperBench IterativeAgent roughly doubles o1 (13.2->24.4), MLE-bench AIDE 8.7% vs OpenHands 4.4%/MLAB 0.8%. Contradiction: scaffold effects are model-dependent (Claude 3.5 Sonnet better with BasicAgent than o1, worse with Iterative) and an unscaffolded long-context model matched tuned scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified (38% vs 32%). Also gains are partly extra compute/time, not separable.

challenges.query: simple scaffold matches complex agent scaffold benchmark agentless simple baseline outperforms agent framework research tasks

text: Independent evaluations of end-to-end autonomous 'AI scientist' systems find substantial quality failures (e.g., flawed experiments, poor novelty checks) that undercut claims of research-level performance.
note: Independent evaluation (Beel et al.) found 42% of experiments failed from coding errors and poor novelty assessment; Sakana's own v2 result: 1 of 3 workshop papers cleared reviewer threshold, none met their internal main-track bar. Counter-evidence (one workshop acceptance; Beel calls it a leap forward) shows progress but does not refute quality failures. Neither compares against a single well-prompted model.
